claim: This study reports the first results of widefield imaging of genetically encoded calcium indicator (GCaMP6f) signals from V1 of behaving macaques.
source: Here we report the first results of widefield imaging of genetically encoded calcium indicator (GCaMP6f) signals from V1 of behaving macaques.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the novelty of the work.

claim: Widefield GCaMP6f imaging provides a robust readout of visual population responses at the columnar scale over multiple mm2 and over several months.
source: This technique provides a robust readout of visual population responses at the columnar scale over multiple mm2 and over several months.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing stable signals over time and spatial extent.

claim: The measured tuning properties of the GCaMP signals to stimulus contrast, orientation and spatial position closely match the predictions of a computational model.
source: The measured tuning properties of the GCaMP signals to stimulus contrast, orientation and spatial position closely match the predictions of the model, suggesting that widefield GCaMP signals are linearly related to the summed local spiking activity.
evidence: Comparison between model predictions and experimental measurements shown in figures.

claim: Widefield GCaMP signals are linearly related to the summed local spiking activity.
source: The measured tuning properties of the GCaMP signals to stimulus contrast, orientation and spatial position closely match the predictions of the model, suggesting that widefield GCaMP signals are linearly related to the summed local spiking activity.
evidence: Inferred from the match between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: In primate primary visual cortex (V1), the smallest localized stimulus activates an area of multiple mm2.
source: For example, in primate primary visual cortex (V1), the smallest localized stimulus activates an area of multiple mm2 (Hubel and Wiesel, 1974; Palmer et al., 2012; Van Essen et al., 1984), a region containing millions of neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A region of multiple mm2 in primate V1 contains millions of neurons.
source: For example, in primate primary visual cortex (V1), the smallest localized stimulus activates an area of multiple mm2 (Hubel and Wiesel, 1974; Palmer et al., 2012; Van Essen et al., 1984), a region containing millions of neurons.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cortical neuron density.

claim: Current techniques for measuring neural activity in behaving animals suffer from a fundamental tradeoff between resolution and coverage.
source: Current techniques for measuring neural activity in behaving animals suffer from a fundamental tradeoff between resolution (spatial and temporal) and coverage, such that, even in a simple perceptual task with a localized stimulus, no single technique can measure the activity of all potentially relevant neurons in a given cortical area with single neuron resolution.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of current imaging techniques.

claim: Beyond an early study with limited success, there are no reports of successful use of genetically encoded reporters in the macaque prior to this work.
source: Beyond an early study with limited success (Heider et al., 2010), there are no reports of successful use of genetically encoded reporters in the macaque.
evidence: Supported by citation and literature review.

claim: Macaque V1 is arguably the most studied and best characterized cortical area in the primate brain.
source: Macaque V1 is arguably the most studied and best characterized cortical area in the primate brain.
evidence: Based on established scientific consensus.

claim: Macaque V1 has a large-scale retinotopic map.
source: An important feature of macaque V1 is its topographic organization, which includes a large-scale retinotopic map (Adams and Horton, 2003; Van Essen et al., 1984; Yang et al., 2007) and a finer scale orientation map (Bonhoeffer and Grinvald, 1991; Chen et al., 2012; Hubel and Wiesel, 1963).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Macaque V1 has a finer scale orientation map.
source: An important feature of macaque V1 is its topographic organization, which includes a large-scale retinotopic map (Adams and Horton, 2003; Van Essen et al., 1984; Yang et al., 2007) and a finer scale orientation map (Bonhoeffer and Grinvald, 1991; Chen et al., 2012; Hubel and Wiesel, 1963).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The topographic organization of the orientation map at the columnar scale is absent from rodent V1.
source: The topographic organization of the orientation map at the columnar scale, which is absent from rodent V1 (Ohki et al., 2005), together with the existing extensive knowledge of the tuning properties of V1 neurons, make macaque V1 an ideal testbed for new imaging techniques and for studying the link between locally pooled neural population responses and single neuron responses.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Serotype 1 rAAVs and CaMKIIα promoter were selected for expressing GCaMP based on preliminary measurements.
source: Based on preliminary measurements, we selected serotype 1 rAAVs and CaMKIIα promoter (Dittgen et al., 2004) for expressing GCaMP.
evidence: Based on experimental testing of different viral vectors.

claim: Six to seven weeks post-injection, high levels of transgene expression could be observed over an area of ~6–10 mm2 per injection site.
source: Six to seven weeks post-injection, high levels of transgene expression could be observed over an area of ~6–10 mm2 per injection site (Figure 2A).
evidence: Directly measured from imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Approximately 80 percent of cells at the injection site were CaMKIIα-positive and therefore excitatory.
source: Based on in situ hybridization analysis of gene expression at the injection site in one animal, approximately 80 percent of cells were CaMKIIα-positive and, therefore, excitatory.
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: All neurons expressing GCaMP were CaMKIIα-positive, attesting to the fidelity of the viral promoter.
source: Further, all neurons expressing GCaMP were CaMKIIα-positive, attesting to the fidelity of the viral promoter (Figure 3).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was no evidence of apoptotic neurons 10 weeks post-injection as judged by Hoechst 33342 staining.
source: There was no evidence of apoptotic neurons, as judged by Hoechst 33342 staining 10 weeks post-injection (not shown).
evidence: Based on histological staining data.

claim: Clear GCaMP signals were entrained on each stimulus cycle when high contrast sinusoidal grating stimuli were flashed at 4 Hz.
source: Clear GCaMP signals were entrained on each stimulus cycle (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B time course data.

claim: GCaMP signals provided a robust readout of visual responses with a high signal to noise ratio.
source: These signals provided a robust readout of visual responses with a high signal to noise ratio (SNR), which was stable for up to six months (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A with d' measurements over time.

claim: GCaMP signals were stable for up to six months.
source: These signals provided a robust readout of visual responses with a high signal to noise ratio (SNR), which was stable for up to six months (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A with measurements over ~200 days.

claim: The pairwise correlations between orientation maps changed smoothly from positive values for maps produced by nearby orientations to negative values for maps produced by orthogonal orientations.
source: As expected from the known structure of orientation maps in V1, the pairwise correlations changed smoothly from positive values for maps produced by nearby orientations to negative values for maps produced by orthogonal orientations.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2D and consistent with known V1 organization.

claim: The composite orientation maps reveal the semi-periodic organization of the orientation map, including the orientation pinwheels.
source: This composite map reveals the semi-periodic organization of the orientation map, including the orientation pinwheels (see inset) (Bonhoeffer and Grinvald, 1991).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2E with visible pinwheel structures.

claim: The converted orientation maps are consistent with maps obtained from the same region with VSD imaging.
source: The converted orientation maps are consistent with maps obtained from the same region with VSD imaging and were stable for several months (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4B-E with correlation measurements.

claim: The converted orientation maps were stable for several months.
source: The converted orientation maps are consistent with maps obtained from the same region with VSD imaging and were stable for several months (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C-D with maps at different time points.

claim: Widefield measurements may reflect calcium signals due to spikes as well as calcium signals due to synaptic potentials in dendrites.
source: This relationship is difficult to predict because the widefield measurements may reflect calcium signals due to spikes as well as calcium signals due to synaptic potentials in dendrites.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential sources of GCaMP signals.

claim: It is possible that the spike-to-calcium nonlinearities in single neurons average out when pooling responses over many heterogeneous neurons.
source: For example, in the present case, it is possible that the spike-to-calcium nonlinearities in single neurons (e.g., Akerboom et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013) average out when pooling responses over many heterogeneous neurons, leading to widefield GCaMP signals that are linearly related to the summed local spiking activity.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: The orientation tuning curve contains an orientation selective component and a large non-selective component.
source: The orientation tuning curve contains an orientation selective component and a large non-selective component, reflecting the fact that the local GCaMP signal pools responses from an area with a heterogeneous population of neurons (see below).
evidence: Observed in Figure 2F and explained by pooling over heterogeneous neurons.

claim: The GCaMP response was weak at low contrasts (<12%) and increased monotonically at higher contrasts.
source: The response was weak at low contrasts (<12%) and increased monotonically at higher contrasts.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2G contrast tuning curve.

claim: The GCaMP responses dropped rapidly as the stimulus' representation deviated from the recorded ROI's location.
source: The GCaMP responses dropped rapidly as the stimulus' representation deviated from the recorded ROI's location, and no responses were observed when the distance exceeded 2 mm (Figure 2H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2H position tuning curve.

claim: No GCaMP responses were observed when the cortical distance exceeded 2 mm.
source: The GCaMP responses dropped rapidly as the stimulus' representation deviated from the recorded ROI's location, and no responses were observed when the distance exceeded 2 mm (Figure 2H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2H position tuning curve.

claim: Recent results suggest that local VSD signals in behaving monkeys reflect the membrane potential of cortical neurons pooled over a Gaussian shaped region with a space constant of ~200 µM.
source: Recent results suggest that local VSD signals in behaving monkeys reflect the membrane potential of cortical neurons pooled over a Gaussian shaped region with a space constant of ~200 µM (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The pooling of VSD signals is likely to be primarily caused by lateral spread of neural processes.
source: This pooling is likely to be primarily caused by lateral spread of neural processes—a small volume of cortical tissue contains axons and dendrites of neurons whose somata can be located several hundred microns away (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: Inference supported by citation.

claim: The pooling area is comparable for widefield imaging of VSD and GCaMP signals.
source: Here we assume that this pooling area is comparable for widefield imaging of VSD and GCaMP signals.
evidence: Assumption made for modeling purposes.

claim: Due to the threshold nonlinearity between membrane potential and spiking activity in single neurons, stimuli that produce weak or moderate membrane potential response elicit almost no spiking activity.
source: Due to the threshold nonlinearity between membrane potential and spiking activity in single neurons (Priebe and Ferster, 2008), stimuli that produce weak or moderate membrane potential response elicit almost no spiking activity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature.

claim: The spiking responses of V1 neurons are more narrowly tuned for orientation and position and are less sensitive to low contrasts than membrane potential responses.
source: Therefore, the spiking responses of V1 neurons are more narrowly tuned for orientation and position and are less sensitive to low contrasts (Priebe and Ferster, 2008).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature.

claim: The spike threshold nonlinearity causes spiking activity to have a smaller non-orientation-selective response relative to membrane potential.
source: In addition, the spike threshold nonlinearity causes spiking activity to have a smaller non-orientation-selective response relative to membrane potential (Priebe and Ferster, 2008).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature.

claim: A comparison of VSD and GCaMP responses is largely consistent with the predictions that GCaMP signals measure primarily the locally pooled spiking activity.
source: A comparison of VSD (red symbols, Figure 6A–C; thin red curves show results from two monkeys separately) and GCaMP responses is largely consistent with these predictions, suggesting that the GCaMP signal may be proportional to the locally summed spiking activity.
evidence: Comparison shown in Figure 6A-C supports the hypothesis.

claim: The latency of the VSD signal is shorter than the latency of the GCaMP signal.
source: The latency of the VSD signal is shorter than the latency of the GCaMP signal.
evidence: Shown in Figure 9E comparing time courses.

claim: The slope of the rising edge of the VSD signal is steeper than the slope of the rising edge of the GCaMP signal.
source: Similarly, the slope of the rising edge of the VSD signal is steeper than the slope of the rising edge of the GCaMP signal.
evidence: Shown in Figure 9E comparing time courses.

claim: The GCaMP signal falls off more slowly than the VSD signal.
source: The GCaMP signal falls off more slowly than the VSD signal, consistent with the differences in the buildup.
evidence: Shown in Figure 9E comparing falling edges.

claim: The GCaMP signal is about five times larger than the VSD signal.
source: The GCaMP signal is about five times larger than the VSD signal, but the two signals are comparable in terms of their sensitivity (d').
evidence: Shown in Figure 9F comparing amplitudes.

claim: GCaMP and VSD signals are comparable in terms of their sensitivity (d').
source: The GCaMP signal is about five times larger than the VSD signal, but the two signals are comparable in terms of their sensitivity (d').
evidence: Shown in Figure 9F comparing d' values.

claim: GCaMP signals are less sensitive to contrast and are more selective to position and orientation than VSD signals.
source: We found that GCaMP signals are less sensitive to contrast and are more selective to position and orientation than VSD signals.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6 comparing tuning curves.

claim: The general agreement between the model's predictions and empirical results supports the hypothesis that widefield GCaMP and VSD signals in V1 of behaving monkeys reflect the linearly summed local neural population activity at the level spiking activity and membrane potential, respectively.
source: The general agreement between the model's predictions and our empirical results supports this hypothesis and provides means to link neural signals measured at different spatial scales and with different techniques.
evidence: Comparison between model and data shown in Figure 8.

claim: This study represents several key advancements over a recent study using similar techniques in anesthetized ferrets.
source: Our study represents several key advancements over a recent study using similar techniques in anesthetized ferrets (Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison with prior work cited.

claim: The experiments in this study are performed in behaving primates that are an important and widely used model system.
source: First, our experiments are performed in behaving primates that are an important and widely used model system.
evidence: Statement about the experimental model used.

claim: This study performs longitudinal measurements over several months, rather than acute experiments.
source: Second, we perform longitudinal measurements over several months, rather than acute experiments.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A with measurements over ~200 days.

claim: This study develops a computational model that quantitatively links widefield measurements with single unit measurements.
source: Third, we develop a computational model that quantitatively links widefield measurements with single unit measurements and provides evidence that the widefield GCaMP signals are dominated by the summed spiking activity of local populations of neurons.
evidence: Model described in Figure 7 and results in Figure 8.

claim: The amplitude of the GCaMP signal is nearly an order of magnitude larger than that of VSD or intrinsic imaging.
source: The amplitude of the GCaMP signal is nearly an order of magnitude larger than that of VSD or intrinsic imaging (Figure 9F).
evidence: Shown in Figure 9F comparing signal amplitudes.

claim: The GCAMP signal has much higher temporal resolution than intrinsic imaging.
source: The GCAMP signal has much higher temporal resolution than intrinsic imaging (Figure 2B), although somewhat less than VSD imaging (Figure 9).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B and Figure 9 comparing time courses.

claim: The GCAMP signal has somewhat less temporal resolution than VSD imaging.
source: The GCAMP signal has much higher temporal resolution than intrinsic imaging (Figure 2B), although somewhat less than VSD imaging (Figure 9).
evidence: Shown in Figure 9 comparing time courses.

claim: A single viral injection procedure generates stable expression of a calcium indicator for many months.
source: In GCaMP imaging, a single viral injection procedure generates stable expression of a calcium indicator for many months (Figure 4).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A with measurements over ~200 days.

claim: GCaMP signals are less susceptible to bleaching than VSD signals.
source: GCaMP signals are also less susceptible to bleaching than VSD signals, accommodating longer and more frequent imaging sessions.
evidence: Based on experimental observations during imaging sessions.

claim: Chronic widefield GCaMP imaging in behaving animals is likely to become a widely used and powerful technique.
source: Thus, chronic widefield GCaMP imaging in behaving animals is likely to become a widely used and powerful technique.
evidence: Speculative prediction based on the advantages demonstrated.

claim: The quantitative measurements and computational model suggest that widefield GCaMP signals reflect the pooled spiking activity of layer 2/3 neurons rather than their pooled synaptic potentials or pre-synaptic inputs.
source: Our quantitative measurements of the tuning properties of the widefield GCaMP signals and our computational model suggest that these signals reflect the pooled spiking activity of layer 2/3 neurons rather than their pooled synaptic potentials or pre-synaptic inputs.
evidence: Supported by model-data comparison in Figure 8.

claim: Had the GCaMP widefield signal been dominated by synaptic potentials in dendrites or pre-synaptic inputs, their tuning properties should have matched those obtained with VSD.
source: Had the GCaMP widefield signal been dominated by synaptic potentials in dendrites or pre-synaptic inputs, their tuning properties should have matched those obtained with VSD.
evidence: Logical inference from the expected properties of different signal sources.

claim: The large and consistent differences between the tuning properties of the widefield GCaMP and VSD signals support the conclusion that the widefield GCaMP signal is tightly linked to the local spikes in layer 2/3.
source: The large and consistent differences between the tuning properties of the widefield GCaMP and VSD signals (Figure 6), and the match between the model's predictions and the observed tuning properties (Figure 8), support the conclusion that the widefield GCaMP signal is tightly linked to the local spikes in layer 2/3.
evidence: Supported by data in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: Comparably tuned dendritic and somatic GCaMP6 signals have been recorded in rodent V1 using two-photon imaging.
source: Comparably tuned dendritic and somatic GCaMP6 signals have been recorded in rodent V1 using two-photon imaging (Chen et al., 2013), and we have obtained similar results in two-photon GCaMP6 experiments in macaque V1 (Nauhaus, Ko, Chen and Seidemann, unpublished observations).
evidence: Supported by citation and unpublished observations.

claim: Similar results to rodent V1 have been obtained in two-photon GCaMP6 experiments in macaque V1.
source: Comparably tuned dendritic and somatic GCaMP6 signals have been recorded in rodent V1 using two-photon imaging (Chen et al., 2013), and we have obtained similar results in two-photon GCaMP6 experiments in macaque V1 (Nauhaus, Ko, Chen and Seidemann, unpublished observations).
evidence: Based on unpublished observations by the authors.

claim: Stimulus-evoked dendritic GCaMP signals may be more correlated with the spiking output of layer 2/3 cells than with their synaptic inputs.
source: Therefore, stimulus-evoked dendritic GCaMP signals may be more correlated with the spiking output of layer 2/3 cells than with their synaptic inputs.
evidence: Inference based on the observed tuning properties.

claim: Factors promoting dendritic GCaMP signals with tuning properties more similar to the spiking output than to the synaptic input could include backpropagating action potentials.
source: Factors promoting dendritic GCaMP signals with tuning properties that are more similar to the spiking output than to the synaptic input could include backpropagating action potentials (Larkum et al., 2007; Waters et al., 2003), as well as nonlinear dendritic NMDA mechanisms (Major et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Factors promoting dendritic GCaMP signals with tuning properties more similar to the spiking output than to the synaptic input could include nonlinear dendritic NMDA mechanisms.
source: Factors promoting dendritic GCaMP signals with tuning properties that are more similar to the spiking output than to the synaptic input could include backpropagating action potentials (Larkum et al., 2007; Waters et al., 2003), as well as nonlinear dendritic NMDA mechanisms (Major et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: The VSD signal is proportional to membrane surface area, while the GCaMP signal is proportional to cytosolic volume.
source: Another important factor that is likely to contribute to the differences between the tuning properties of the widefield GCaMP and VSD signals is that the VSD signal is proportional to membrane surface area, while the GCaMP signal is proportional to cytosolic volume.
evidence: Based on the known properties of VSD and GCaMP indicators.

claim: Preliminary results from two-photon imaging in anesthetized macaque expressing GCaMP6f show healthy neurons and characteristic paranuclear responses to visual stimuli.
source: Indeed, preliminary results from two-photon imaging in anesthetized macaque expressing GCaMP6f show healthy neurons and characteristic paranuclear responses to visual stimuli, indicating that GCaMP imaging at cellular resolution can complement widefield imaging at the same anatomical location (Nauhaus, Ko, Chen and Seidemann, unpublished observations).
evidence: Based on unpublished observations by the authors.

claim: GCaMP imaging at cellular resolution can complement widefield imaging at the same anatomical location.
source: Indeed, preliminary results from two-photon imaging in anesthetized macaque expressing GCaMP6f show healthy neurons and characteristic paranuclear responses to visual stimuli, indicating that GCaMP imaging at cellular resolution can complement widefield imaging at the same anatomical location (Nauhaus, Ko, Chen and Seidemann, unpublished observations).
evidence: Inference from preliminary two-photon imaging results.

claim: Combining widefield and two-photon GCaMP imaging in the same animal over extended periods of time should help resolve many of the remaining questions regarding the relationship between neural responses measured over different spatial scales.
source: Combining widefield and two-photon GCaMP imaging in the same animal over extended periods of time should help resolve many of the remaining questions regarding the relationship between neural responses measured over different spatial scales.
evidence: Speculative prediction about future research directions.

claim: Combining complementary empirical measurements with realistic computational models will provide unprecedented access to distributed neural responses in behaving subjects.
source: Combining complementary empirical measurements with realistic computational models that interpolate fine-scale and large-scale measurements will provide unprecedented access to distributed neural responses in behaving subjects, leading to a deeper understanding of neural population coding in the brain.
evidence: Speculative prediction about future research directions.

claim: Typical viral titers were >1010 genomes/microliter.
source: Typical titers were >1010 genomes/microliter.
evidence: Measurement of viral preparation.

claim: Virus was deposited at depths of 1.5, 1.0 and 0.5 mm (0.5 µl per site).
source: Virus was deposited at depths of 1.5, 1.0 and 0.5 mm (0.5 µl per site) using a positive displacement microinjector (Nanoject II).
evidence: Description of injection protocol.

claim: GCaMP fluorescence was observed 40 days following injection.
source: GCaMP fluorescence was observed 40 days following injection, peaking around 75 days, and remained constant for up to 190 days after injection (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A tracking expression over time.

claim: GCaMP fluorescence peaked around 75 days after injection.
source: GCaMP fluorescence was observed 40 days following injection, peaking around 75 days, and remained constant for up to 190 days after injection (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A tracking expression over time.

claim: GCaMP fluorescence remained constant for up to 190 days after injection.
source: GCaMP fluorescence was observed 40 days following injection, peaking around 75 days, and remained constant for up to 190 days after injection (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A tracking expression over time.

claim: In a field of view containing 232 cells, 185 (80%) were CaMKIIα(+); of these, 168 (91%) were GCaMP(+) and 17 (9%) were GCaMP(-); none was CaMKIIα(-)/GCaMP(+).
source: In a field of view containing 232 cells, 185 (80%) were CaMKIIα(+); of these, 168 (91%) were GCaMP(+) and 17 (9%) were GCaMP(-); none was CaMKIIα(-)/GCaMP(+).
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Eye position was monitored by an infrared eye tracker.
source: Eye position was monitored by an infrared eye tracker (Dr. Bouis or EyeLink).
evidence: Description of experimental methods.

claim: The mean luminance of the screen was maintained at 30 cd/m2.
source: The mean luminance of the screen was maintained at 30 cd/m2.
evidence: Description of stimulus parameters.

claim: Data acquisition was time locked to the animal's heartbeat.
source: Data acquisition was time locked to the animal's heartbeat.
evidence: Description of imaging methods.

claim: Imaging was performed at 20 Hz for GCaMP imaging and 100 Hz for VSD imaging.
source: Imaging was performed at 20 Hz for GCaMP imaging and 100 Hz for VSD imaging.
evidence: Description of imaging parameters.

claim: The model of membrane-potential and spiking activity is based on tuning parameter values of single V1 neurons measured by the authors and by others.
source: The model of membrane-potential and spiking activity is based on tuning parameter values of single V1 neurons measured by us and by others (see Table 1).
evidence: Model parameters listed in Table 1 with citations.
